prompt.context: Your firm has won an RFP to help a domestic airline carrier examine their in-flight connectivity (IFC) strategy. With 80% of US-based aircraft already outfitted with IFC technology and competitive pressures rising, offering WiFi service is becoming table-stakes. Your client has yet to enter the game, but they know it's something they need to consider to stay competitive.
prompt.question: What are some of the key things the client should think about when assessing their go-to-market strategy for IFC?

clarifying_info.q: What routes does the airline fly?
clarifying_info.a: The airline flies primarily domestic routes within the continental US, as well as select flights to Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.

clarifying_info.q: What does IFC include — is it the same as in-flight entertainment?
clarifying_info.a: IFC includes only WiFi connectivity. In-flight entertainment (IFE) is delivered via an on-board server through a separate system, but the two can be integrated into one user experience.

clarifying_info.q: What is the airline's primary objective?
clarifying_info.a: The airline's main objective is to stay competitive.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the fleet and how many flights does the airline operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline has 90 planes and services approximately 30,000 flights per year.

IFC is typically installed and managed by an outside vendor, either through a branded service (e.g., GoGoAir) or a wholesale, white-label solution (e.g., Row44). Contracts are typically 10+ years long.

clarifying_info.q: Are all vendor technologies the same?
clarifying_info.a: Different vendors use different technologies, which vary in quality.

clarifying_info.q: How does bandwidth work with more users?
clarifying_info.a: Total bandwidth is shared across passengers, so the more passengers buy a session, the slower the service. Some carriers intentionally charge high prices to limit usage and ensure better service.

framework: Pricing and pricing model (free, ad-supported, pay per data usage, pay per time, pay by speed tier, subscription)
Market demand: take rate and market segments
Costs: upfront capital investment and ongoing operating costs
Vendor contract structure: revenue/business model, investment cost split, branding, contract length, technology
Product and user experience: built-in screens vs. BYO-screen, white-label vs. vendor branding, speeds, IFE interoperability, add-ons (calling/texting)
Technology: speed, bandwidth, latency, water-coverage availability
Go-to-market: rollout timing, marketing, crew training, ad sales

questions.prompt: Your analyst pulled benchmarks on what two competitors are doing today (Exhibit 1). What are your thoughts on these two models?
questions.guidance:
Candidate should compare pros and cons of each model rather than just summarizing the table, and should flag that the exhibit omits critical info (cost structure, technology, product features, IFE interoperability). Strong candidates will consider structures beyond the two shown and discuss which model better fits the client.

Competitor 1 (Vendor-branded, revenue share, $25/session set by vendor):
- Pros: less operational burden on airline, potential for customer experience continuity across carriers (e.g., subscriptions), limited upfront costs
- Cons: limited airline control over pricing (high price could suppress take rates and anger customers), brand fit/identity concerns

Competitor 2 (Airline-branded, wholesale, free for customers):
- Pros: full control over pricing and user experience, potential for better ROI, easier integration with airline's other products (e.g., IFE)
- Cons: more operational burden on airline, higher costs

Other considerations: who pays the initial investment, ongoing cost structure, potential to adopt more than one model across the fleet, technology limitations (vendors differ in quality).

questions.prompt: The client has decided to partner with a white-label IFC vendor to outfit all 90 planes. The airline and vendor will share the initial investment; then the airline pays the vendor a per-session fee covering operating expenses. What percentage of passengers need to purchase a session for the airline to break even in 2 years? Additional data (give only when asked): Capex = $250K per plane (airline covers 40%); Margin = $10 per session net of the per-session vendor fee. Assume 100% seat occupancy and all aircraft outfitted simultaneously.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up a clean breakeven equation: total investment / (total passengers x margin per session). Strong candidates will proactively question the 100% occupancy assumption and ask about ad revenue treatment. The resulting ~12.9% take rate is above current market rates of 5-10%, so strong candidates will flag this and discuss implications.

math.setup: Break-even condition: Total passengers over 2 years × take rate × $10/session = Total airline investment
steps: Airline share of capex per plane: $250K × 40% = $100K/plane
Wide body passengers (2 yrs): 300 seats × 2,500 flights/yr × 2 yrs = 1.5M
Narrow body passengers (2 yrs): 100 seats × 27,500 flights/yr × 2 yrs = 5.5M
Solve for take rate: 7M × take rate × $10 = $9M → take rate = $9M / $70M = 12.86% ≈ 12.9%
math.answer: ~12.9% take rate required to break even in 2 years

questions.prompt: Market research shows take rates are only 5–10% today for paid connectivity. The client is concerned about hitting the break-even target. What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?
questions.guidance:
This is a correlation question: what variables are correlated with higher take rates? Candidate should brainstorm multiple categories and hypothesize the direction each variable needs to swing to increase take rate. Strong candidates cover all three categories below and add directional commentary (e.g., longer flights → higher take rate; lower price → higher take rate).

Flight characteristics: flight length (longer = higher take rate), time of day (daytime vs. red-eye), availability of other entertainment systems
Product characteristics: price, speeds available, quality of service, number of connected devices allowed
Passenger characteristics: age, gender, income, cabin class (business vs. economy), purpose of travel (business vs. leisure)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers of IFC take rate?

categories.name: Flight characteristics
ideas: Flight length (longer flights correlate with higher take rate)
Time of day (daytime flights vs. red-eyes)
Availability of other in-flight entertainment options

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: Number of devices a session covers

recommendation: The airline should partner with a wholesale, white-label vendor to retain control over pricing and the user experience.
Roll-out across the fleet should be gradual, beginning with a pilot program to optimize pricing, user experience, and operations.
Roll-out should prioritize newer planes on routes with high expected take rates.
risks: Due to the large upfront investment, contracts are likely to run 10+ years, making smart vendor selection extremely critical.
Difficult to strike the right balance between maximizing revenue and maintaining a sufficiently low take rate to ensure higher connection speeds.
IFC technology is still nascent, creating potential for poor user experience that damages the brand.
next_steps: Aircraft prioritization (route analysis to identify highest-take-rate routes)
Pilot program launch and performance monitoring
